screens.title: Linear Algebra for Robotics
screens.narratorSegment: In robotics we speak the language of coordinates. Over the next screens you'll learn how vectors describe points and directions, how matrices encode rotations and other linear transforms, and how homogeneous matrices let us combine rotation and translation into a single chainable operation. These ideas let a robot take a measurement made by a camera or sensor and express it in the robot's body frame or in the world frame so the system can reason and act. You'll see concrete matrix formulas, a practical MATLAB example, and the algebraic shortcuts that make transforms efficient to compute. I'll also point out common misconceptions, like treating 3D rotations as commutative or forgetting to use homogeneous coordinates when combining rotation and translation. By the end you will be able to write and chain transforms, invert them efficiently, and reason about dot products, cross products, determinants, and when SVD matters. Think of this chapter as the toolkit you use whenever you need to move a point between frames. Ask yourself: which frame is the measurement expressed in before you start to multiply?

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: Vectors and matrices provide a consistent language to represent positions and orientations; homogeneous transforms let you chain and invert frame-to-frame conversions efficiently.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Linear Algebra for Robotics
Overview

Why coordinates matter

Every measurement and command in a robot is relative to a frame. Vectors give positions and directions. Matrices rotate, scale, or reflect. Homogeneous matrices combine rotation and translation so you can chain transforms with matrix multiplication.

Vectors
Position & direction
Rotations
Rx, Ry, Rz
Transforms
Chain & invert
In this lesson
You will learn how to write rotation matrices, create homogeneous transforms, chain them, compute inverses more efficiently, and apply dot and cross products in robotics tasks.
Coming up: rotation matrices, Euler conventions, MATLAB example.
Visual concept

Frames and chained transforms

Static visualization
World frame
Origin, axes fixed. Points here are global coordinates.
Example point: p_world = [2, 1, 0]^T
Body & camera
Body is translated and rotated relative to world. Camera is offset from body.
Chain: T_world_body · T_body_camera = T_world_camera
Key Takeaway

Start every transform by identifying which frame each vector is expressed in. Mixing frames causes the most common mistakes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These four objectives give you focused, assessable skills. First, you'll represent positions, orientations, and coordinate transforms using vectors and matrices so you can change how a point is expressed between frames. Second, you'll construct and apply rotation matrices in 2D and 3D, which lets you rotate sensor measurements into a common orientation. Third, you'll combine rotations and translations into homogeneous transformations and chain them reliably, which is how robots compute poses across multiple linked frames. Fourth, you will compute inverses, determinants, and eigenvalues used to check rotations, invert transforms efficiently, and analyze system properties. For each objective you'll see a short mnemonic, a competency milestone, and a concrete example so you can practice. These objectives focus on doing real frame arithmetic, not just memorizing formulas. That practical focus is what makes coordinate transforms reliable in robot systems.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Tools
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond formulas, you'll practice by writing and chaining transformations in code and by checking properties that confirm correct rotations. The exercises include a MATLAB script where you define world, body, and camera frames, transform a camera point into world coordinates, and then invert the transform to recover the original point. You will also apply determinant checks to detect reflections or scaling and use dot and cross products to compute angles and normals. These practical checks are critical. Robots often fail not because the math is unknown, but because frames are mixed or a transpose was used in the wrong place. As you practice, use small unit checks: confirm that a rotation matrix times its transpose equals the identity and that determinant equals one. These simple tests catch many bugs before they affect physical systems.

Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Practice & Tools
Practice checklist
Unit test
Verify R * R' equals the identity within numerical tolerance to confirm orthogonality.
Determinant
Check det(R) is 1 to ensure no reflection or scaling was introduced.
Round-trip
Apply a transform and its inverse to a point and verify you recover the original coordinates.
These quick checks form the foundation for confident coordinate arithmetic.

screens.title: Vectors and Coordinate Frames
screens.narratorSegment: A vector is an ordered list of numbers that represents a point or a direction. In robotics we commonly use a 3D position vector p = [x, y, z]^T to express where an object or sensor is relative to a coordinate frame. A coordinate frame consists of three orthogonal axes and an origin; every measurement is relative to some frame, such as the robot body, a sensor, or the world. Concretely, if your camera reports a point p_camera = [0.5, 0.3, 2.0]^T, that vector has no meaning until you specify the camera frame. A common misconception is to treat vectors as absolute; instead always annotate the frame. One simple practice is to name vectors with a frame subscript, for example p_world or p_camera, and only transform between them using matrices. Example: if the camera is mounted 0.1 meters forward and 0.05 meters up in the body frame, that offset is a 3×1 translation vector used in a homogeneous transform. Takeaway: label frames explicitly and carry that label through every computation. Question to reflect on: when you get a measurement from a sensor, what frame is it expressed in and what transform do you need to bring it into your control frame?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Vectors encode positions or directions; coordinate frames give vectors context and must be tracked explicitly.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Vectors & Frames
What is a vector?
A vector is an ordered list of numbers that represents either a position or a direction relative to a coordinate frame.
Example position vector
p = [x; y; z]  % column vector in a frame
Mnemonic: Always attach a frame label, e.g., p_camera or p_world.
Coordinate frame

A frame defines axis directions and an origin. Measurements without a frame are ambiguous. Transformations map vectors from one frame to another.

Concrete scenario
A camera reports p_camera = [0.5;0.3;2.0]. To plan movement in world coordinates, you must transform that vector into the world frame using a homogeneous transform.
Key Takeaway
Label frames and never mix vectors from different frames without an explicit transform.

screens.title: Matrices as Linear Transformations
screens.narratorSegment: A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers that represents a linear mapping from one vector space to another. In robotics the most important matrices are rotation matrices, which preserve lengths and angles, but it's useful to remember matrices can also represent scaling, shear, and projection. The key property of a linear transform is that it distributes over vector addition and scales with scalar multiplication. Practically, applying a matrix to a vector applies the same linear rule across all points, so you can rotate or scale entire point sets by multiplying each vector. A common misconception is to treat every transformation as linear; translations are not linear in the pure vector sense, which is why homogeneous coordinates extend vectors so translations can be represented as a matrix multiplication in a higher-dimensional space. Example: applying a 3×3 rotation matrix R to a vector p gives a rotated vector Rp. Takeaway: use matrices for consistent, repeatable linear mappings, and if you need translations too, move to homogeneous form. Matrices as Linear Transformations means matrices apply linear, repeatable maps to vectors; rotations are orthogonal matrices that preserve length and angle.. In practical terms, how matrices rotate, scale, and map vectors between spaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Matrix role
keyIdea.text: Matrices apply linear, repeatable maps to vectors; rotations are orthogonal matrices that preserve length and angle.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Matrices as Linear Transforms
What a matrix does

A matrix maps input vectors to output vectors by a fixed linear rule. For rotations, that rule preserves vector lengths and angles.

Property
If R is a rotation, then R * R' = I and det(R) = 1.
Example: rotation applied
% rotate point p by R:
p_rotated = R * p;
Misconception: translations are not linear. To include translations use homogeneous coordinates and a 4×4 matrix.
Why it matters
Using matrices makes batch operations and chaining efficient, which is essential for real-time robot calculations.

screens.title: 2D Rotation Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: In 2D, rotation is simple and intuitive. The rotation matrix R(theta) rotates a vector by angle theta and is written as [cos(theta) -sin(theta); sin(theta) cos(theta)]. Multiply R(theta) by a column vector p to rotate it. A concrete example: rotate p = [1; 0] by theta = 30 degrees. Compute cos 30° and sin 30° and multiply to get the new coordinates. This operation preserves length: the rotated vector still has the same magnitude. A common slip is to invert rotation by using R(theta) instead of R(-theta); the inverse of a 2D rotation is R(-theta), which equals R(theta)' because rotation matrices are orthogonal. Why this matters: many localization and mapping routines rotate planar observations into a common heading before fusing them. Check your computation by confirming that R * R' is the identity and that the vector length is preserved. Takeaway question: if you rotate a sensor measurement into a global frame and then rotate back with R', what should you recover? 2D Rotation Matrix means r(θ) rotates in the plane; orthogonality means the inverse is its transpose.. In practical terms, rotate a vector by angle θ in the plane. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: 2D rotation
keyIdea.text: R(θ) rotates in the plane; orthogonality means the inverse is its transpose.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › 2D Rotation Matrix
Rotation formula
R(θ) = [ cos(θ)  -sin(θ);
           sin(θ)   cos(θ) ]

p_rot = R(θ) * p
Check orthogonality: R * R' ≈ I
Concrete example
Rotate p = [1; 0] by θ = 30°. cos(30°)=0.866, sin(30°)=0.5. The rotated vector becomes approximately [0.866; 0.5].
Key Takeaway
In 2D rotations preserve magnitude and are inverted by transpose; use this for quick checks.

screens.title: 3D Rotation Matrices: Axes and Construction
screens.narratorSegment: Rotation in 3D is built from basic rotations about the principal axes. For example, a rotation about the z axis by angle theta is Rz(theta) = [[cos, -sin, 0]; [sin, cos, 0]; [0, 0, 1]]. Similar matrices rotate around x and y. Any 3D orientation can be represented by composing these basic rotations. However, order matters: rotating around x then y is different from y then x. A concrete example: rotate a vector pointing along x first about z, then about y, and observe that the final orientation changes if you swap the order. A common misconception is to treat 3D rotations like scalars; they do not commute. In robotics we therefore rely on explicit conventions like roll-pitch-yaw or Z-Y-X Euler angles so everyone agrees on the order. Takeaway: learn the axis rotation matrices and always apply rotations in the specified convention. Try writing a small script that composes Rx, Ry, and Rz in two different orders and compare the results to internalize non-commutativity. 3D Rotation Matrices: Axes and Construction means build 3d orientations by composing rx, ry, and rz; the order of multiplication determines the final orientation.. In practical terms, basic rotations around x, y, and z axes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: 3D rotations
keyIdea.text: Build 3D orientations by composing Rx, Ry, and Rz; the order of multiplication determines the final orientation.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › 3D Rotation Matrices
Axis rotations
Rz(θ) = [ cosθ  -sinθ  0;
           sinθ   cosθ  0;
             0      0   1 ]

% Rx and Ry are similar but rotate about x and y axes
Compose these matrices to build complex 3D orientations.
Order matters
Example: compute R = Ry(α) * Rx(β) and compare to R' = Rx(β) * Ry(α). The two results differ. This is non-commutativity of 3D rotations.
Common mistake
Applying rotations in the wrong order leads to unexpected final orientations. Use explicit conventions like Z-Y-X to avoid ambiguity.

screens.title: Homogeneous Transformation Matrix
screens.narratorSegment: A homogeneous transformation embeds a 3×3 rotation and a 3×1 translation into a 4×4 matrix so both can be applied by a single matrix multiplication to homogeneous coordinates. The matrix T = [R p; 0 1] acts on a homogeneous point [x; y; z; 1]. This lets you chain transformations: multiplying two 4×4 transforms composes their rotations and translations automatically. A practical benefit is that you no longer need to treat rotation and translation separately when transforming points or frames. A misconception is to multiply translations separately or to forget the homogeneous coordinate; failing to use the bottom row [0 0 0 1] breaks chainability. Example: if the body frame is translated and rotated relative to world, and the camera is offset from the body, compute T_world_camera = T_world_body * T_body_camera. Takeaway: move to homogeneous matrices whenever you combine rotation and translation so chains remain simple and consistent. Homogeneous Transformation Matrix means use 4×4 homogeneous matrices to represent rotation and translation together and to enable simple chain multiplication.. In practical terms, combine rotation r and translation p into one 4×4 matrix. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Homogeneous form
keyIdea.text: Use 4×4 homogeneous matrices to represent rotation and translation together and to enable simple chain multiplication.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Homogeneous Transform
Matrix form
T = [ R  p;
      0  1 ]

% Acting on homogeneous point:
p_h = [x; y; z; 1]
p_transformed = T * p_h
Chaining: T_world_camera = T_world_body * T_body_camera
Concrete example
If R rotates 30° about z and p = [1;2;3], then T applies both the rotation and that translation in one multiplication.
Key Takeaway
Homogeneous matrices are the standard tool for combining rotation and translation and for composing frames by multiplication.

screens.title: Chaining Transforms: Camera → Body → World
screens.narratorSegment: Chaining transforms is fundamental: if you know T_world_body and T_body_camera, you can compute T_world_camera by multiplication: T_world_camera = T_world_body * T_body_camera. To transform a point expressed in the camera frame to the world frame, convert the point to homogeneous coordinates and apply T_world_camera. Concretely, if p_camera_homogeneous = [0.5; 0.3; 2.0; 1], then p_world = T_world_camera * p_camera_homogeneous. This composition is associative, so you can precompute compound transforms for efficiency. A practical pitfall is mixing up which direction each transform points. T_AB maps points from B to A, so be careful with subscripts. Another problem is applying transforms in the wrong order; matrix multiplication is not commutative. Example: given T_world_body and T_body_camera from sensors or calibration, chain them and validate by transforming a known point and checking its expected world location. Takeaway: always track the direction of each transform and validate chains using a round-trip inverse test. Chaining Transforms: Camera → Body → World means compose transforms by multiplication while carefully tracking which frame each transform maps between.. In practical terms, compute world coordinates by multiplying transforms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Chaining rule
keyIdea.text: Compose transforms by multiplication while carefully tracking which frame each transform maps between.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › Chaining Transforms
Step-by-step chain
  1. Compute T_world_camera = T_world_body * T_body_camera.
  2. Express p_camera in homogeneous form p_cam_h = [x;y;z;1].
  3. Compute p_world = T_world_camera * p_cam_h.
  4. Validate with a known reference or inverse transform.
Concrete scenario
Given p_camera = [0.5;0.3;2.0;1], and known T_world_body and T_body_camera, compute p_world and verify with a calibration marker in the environment.
Check
Use the inverse transform to map back to camera frame and confirm you recover p_camera.

screens.title: Inverse of a Homogeneous Transform
screens.narratorSegment: The inverse of a homogeneous transform has a special, efficient form. For T = [R p; 0 1] the inverse is T_inv = [R' -R' * p; 0 1], where R' denotes the transpose of R. This formula leverages orthogonality: R' is the inverse of R for rotation matrices. It avoids a general 4×4 inverse computation and is numerically stable for pure rotations. Use this when you know a transform from B to A (T_AB) and need the reverse mapping T_BA. A common mistake is to invert by transposing the entire 4×4 matrix or by neglecting the -R'·p term, which yields incorrect translations. Example: given R and p for a camera relative to body, compute T_body_camera_inv by transposing R and negating R' times p to get T_camera_body. Takeaway: use the R' and -R'·p shortcut to invert homogeneous transforms accurately and efficiently. Try this on your MATLAB script to confirm round-trip accuracy. Inverse of a Homogeneous Transform means for t = [r p; 0 1], compute t_inv = [r' -r' p; 0 1] to invert rotations and translations efficiently.. In practical terms, efficient inverse using r' and -r'·p. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

narration.text: The inverse of a homogeneous transform has a special, efficient form. For T = [R p; 0 1] the inverse is T_inv = [R' -R' * p; 0 1], where R' denotes the transpose of R. This formula leverages orthogonality: R' is the inverse of R for rotation matrices. It avoids a general 4×4 inverse computation and is numerically stable for pure rotations. Use this when you know a transform from B to A (T_AB) and need the reverse mapping T_BA. A common mistake is to invert by transposing the entire 4×4 matrix or by neglecting the -R'·p term, which yields incorrect translations. Example: given R and p for a camera relative to body, compute T_body_camera_inv by transposing R and negating R' times p to get T_camera_body. T_inv = [R'   -R'*p;

screens.title: Dot and Cross Products
screens.narratorSegment: Dot and cross products are simple algebraic tools with direct geometric meaning. The dot product a · b equals |a||b|cos(theta), so it gives the cosine of the angle between two vectors when normalized; this is used to compute alignment or to project one vector onto another. The cross product a × b yields a vector perpendicular to both a and b with magnitude |a||b|sin(theta); in robotics it's used to compute normals, moments, and torques. A concrete example: if a sensor measures a surface normal and you need a tangent direction, cross products give you a perpendicular vector that lies in the tangent plane. A common misconception is confusing component-wise multiplication with dot product; remember dot is a scalar, cross is a vector. Takeaway: use dot to measure alignment and projection, use cross for perpendicular directions and torque computations. Try small numeric examples to build intuition: pick simple orthogonal unit vectors and confirm dot equals zero and cross yields the third axis direction. In practical terms, compute angles, projections, and perpendicular vectors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. screens.title: Determinant, Eigenvalues, and SVD
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond transforms, several matrix properties are important in robotics. The determinant of a rotation matrix should be 1; if it's not, the matrix encodes scaling or reflection and is not a valid pure rotation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors satisfy Av = λv and are useful for analyzing system behavior, such as stability or principal directions. Singular value decomposition, A = U Σ V^T, decomposes a general matrix into orthogonal factors and singular values; SVD is commonly used in solving least-squares problems and in computer vision tasks like essential matrix decomposition. A concrete example: use SVD to compute a least-squares fit for a transform when you have noisy correspondences between frames. A common misconception is to assume eigenvectors always form a basis; this fails for defective matrices but is fine for symmetric and many practical matrices. Takeaway: use determinant as a quick validity check for rotations, use eigen and SVD where decomposition and robust solving are required. Determinant, Eigenvalues, and SVD means use det to validate rotations, eigenanalysis for principal directions, and svd for stable decomposition and least-squares solutions.. keyIdea.text: Build R, form T = [R p; 0 1], transform homogeneous points, and verify with an inverse round-trip.

content.html:
Module 1 › Chapter 1.1 › MATLAB Example
MATLAB code
% Define a rotation of 30 degrees around the z-axis
theta = deg2rad(30);
Rz = [cos(theta) -sin(theta) 0;
      sin(theta)  cos(theta) 0;
      0           0          1];

% Define a translation vector
t = [1; 2; 3];

% Construct the homogeneous transformation matrix
T = [Rz, t; 0, 0, 0, 1];

% Transform a point from the body frame to the world frame
p_body = [0.5; 0.2; 1.0; 1];
p_world = T * p_body;
Remember to use homogeneous coordinates when applying T. Validate by computing the inverse via R' and -R'*p and applying it to p_world to recover p_body.

Keep tests that verify round-trips and orthogonality to catch numerical mistakes early.

fullNarratorScript:
In robotics we speak the language of coordinates. Over the next screens you'll learn how vectors describe points and directions, how matrices encode rotations and other linear transforms, and how homogeneous matrices let us combine rotation and translation into a single chainable operation. These ideas let a robot take a measurement made by a camera or sensor and express it in the robot's body frame or in the world frame so the system can reason and act. You'll see concrete matrix formulas, a practical MATLAB example, and the algebraic shortcuts that make transforms efficient to compute. I'll also point out common misconceptions, like treating 3D rotations as commutative or forgetting to use homogeneous coordinates when combining rotation and translation. By the end you will be able to write and chain transforms, invert them efficiently, and reason about dot products, cross products, determinants, and when SVD matters. Think of this chapter as the toolkit you use whenever you need to move a point between frames. Ask yourself: which frame is the measurement expressed in before you start to multiply?

These four objectives give you focused, assessable skills. First, you'll represent positions, orientations, and coordinate transforms using vectors and matrices so you can change how a point is expressed between frames. Second, you'll construct and apply rotation matrices in 2D and 3D, which lets you rotate sensor measurements into a common orientation. Third, you'll combine rotations and translations into homogeneous transformations and chain them reliably, which is how robots compute poses across multiple linked frames. Fourth, you will compute inverses, determinants, and eigenvalues used to check rotations, invert transforms efficiently, and analyze system properties. For each objective you'll see a short mnemonic, a competency milestone, and a concrete example so you can practice. These objectives focus on doing real frame arithmetic, not just memorizing formulas. That practical focus is what makes coordinate transforms reliable in robot systems.

Beyond formulas, you'll practice by writing and chaining transformations in code and by checking properties that confirm correct rotations. The exercises include a MATLAB script where you define world, body, and camera frames, transform a camera point into world coordinates, and then invert the transform to recover the original point. You will also apply determinant checks to detect reflections or scaling and use dot and cross products to compute angles and normals. These practical checks are critical. Robots often fail not because the math is unknown, but because frames are mixed or a transpose was used in the wrong place. As you practice, use small unit checks: confirm that a rotation matrix times its transpose equals the identity and that determinant equals one. These simple tests catch many bugs before they affect physical systems.

A vector is an ordered list of numbers that represents a point or a direction. In robotics we commonly use a 3D position vector p = [x, y, z]^T to express where an object or sensor is relative to a coordinate frame. A coordinate frame consists of three orthogonal axes and an origin; every measurement is relative to some frame, such as the robot body, a sensor, or the world. Concretely, if your camera reports a point p_camera = [0.5, 0.3, 2.0]^T, that vector has no meaning until you specify the camera frame. A common misconception is to treat vectors as absolute; instead always annotate the frame. One simple practice is to name vectors with a frame subscript, for example p_world or p_camera, and only transform between them using matrices. Example: if the camera is mounted 0.1 meters forward and 0.05 meters up in the body frame, that offset is a 3×1 translation vector used in a homogeneous transform. Takeaway: label frames explicitly and carry that label through every computation. Question to reflect on: when you get a measurement from a sensor, what frame is it expressed in and what transform do you need to bring it into your control frame?

A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers that represents a linear mapping from one vector space to another. In robotics the most important matrices are rotation matrices, which preserve lengths and angles, but it's useful to remember matrices can also represent scaling, shear, and projection. The key property of a linear transform is that it distributes over vector addition and scales with scalar multiplication. Practically, applying a matrix to a vector applies the same linear rule across all points, so you can rotate or scale entire point sets by multiplying each vector. A common misconception is to treat every transformation as linear; translations are not linear in the pure vector sense, which is why homogeneous coordinates extend vectors so translations can be represented as a matrix multiplication in a higher-dimensional space. Example: applying a 3×3 rotation matrix R to a vector p gives a rotated vector Rp. Takeaway: use matrices for consistent, repeatable linear mappings, and if you need translations too, move to homogeneous form. Matrices as Linear Transformations means matrices apply linear, repeatable maps to vectors; rotations are orthogonal matrices that preserve length and angle.. In practical terms, how matrices rotate, scale, and map vectors between spaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

In 2D, rotation is simple and intuitive. The rotation matrix R(theta) rotates a vector by angle theta and is written as [cos(theta) -sin(theta); sin(theta) cos(theta)]. Multiply R(theta) by a column vector p to rotate it. A concrete example: rotate p = [1; 0] by theta = 30 degrees. Compute cos 30° and sin 30° and multiply to get the new coordinates. This operation preserves length: the rotated vector still has the same magnitude. A common slip is to invert rotation by using R(theta) instead of R(-theta); the inverse of a 2D rotation is R(-theta), which equals R(theta)' because rotation matrices are orthogonal. Why this matters: many localization and mapping routines rotate planar observations into a common heading before fusing them. Check your computation by confirming that R * R' is the identity and that the vector length is preserved. Takeaway question: if you rotate a sensor measurement into a global frame and then rotate back with R', what should you recover? 2D Rotation Matrix means r(θ) rotates in the plane; orthogonality means the inverse is its transpose.. In practical terms, rotate a vector by angle θ in the plane. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Rotation in 3D is built from basic rotations about the principal axes. For example, a rotation about the z axis by angle theta is Rz(theta) = [[cos, -sin, 0]; [sin, cos, 0]; [0, 0, 1]]. Similar matrices rotate around x and y. Any 3D orientation can be represented by composing these basic rotations. However, order matters: rotating around x then y is different from y then x. A concrete example: rotate a vector pointing along x first about z, then about y, and observe that the final orientation changes if you swap the order. A common misconception is to treat 3D rotations like scalars; they do not commute. In robotics we therefore rely on explicit conventions like roll-pitch-yaw or Z-Y-X Euler angles so everyone agrees on the order. Takeaway: learn the axis rotation matrices and always apply rotations in the specified convention. Try writing a small script that composes Rx, Ry, and Rz in two different orders and compare the results to internalize non-commutativity. 3D Rotation Matrices: Axes and Construction means build 3d orientations by composing rx, ry, and rz; the order of multiplication determines the final orientation.. In practical terms, basic rotations around x, y, and z axes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A homogeneous transformation embeds a 3×3 rotation and a 3×1 translation into a 4×4 matrix so both can be applied by a single matrix multiplication to homogeneous coordinates. The matrix T = [R p; 0 1] acts on a homogeneous point [x; y; z; 1]. This lets you chain transformations: multiplying two 4×4 transforms composes their rotations and translations automatically. A practical benefit is that you no longer need to treat rotation and translation separately when transforming points or frames. A misconception is to multiply translations separately or to forget the homogeneous coordinate; failing to use the bottom row [0 0 0 1] breaks chainability. Example: if the body frame is translated and rotated relative to world, and the camera is offset from the body, compute T_world_camera = T_world_body * T_body_camera. Takeaway: move to homogeneous matrices whenever you combine rotation and translation so chains remain simple and consistent. Homogeneous Transformation Matrix means use 4×4 homogeneous matrices to represent rotation and translation together and to enable simple chain multiplication.. In practical terms, combine rotation r and translation p into one 4×4 matrix. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Chaining transforms is fundamental: if you know T_world_body and T_body_camera, you can compute T_world_camera by multiplication: T_world_camera = T_world_body * T_body_camera. To transform a point expressed in the camera frame to the world frame, convert the point to homogeneous coordinates and apply T_world_camera. Concretely, if p_camera_homogeneous = [0.5; 0.3; 2.0; 1], then p_world = T_world_camera * p_camera_homogeneous. This composition is associative, so you can precompute compound transforms for efficiency. A practical pitfall is mixing up which direction each transform points. T_AB maps points from B to A, so be careful with subscripts. Another problem is applying transforms in the wrong order; matrix multiplication is not commutative. Example: given T_world_body and T_body_camera from sensors or calibration, chain them and validate by transforming a known point and checking its expected world location. Takeaway: always track the direction of each transform and validate chains using a round-trip inverse test. Chaining Transforms: Camera → Body → World means compose transforms by multiplication while carefully tracking which frame each transform maps between.. In practical terms, compute world coordinates by multiplying transforms. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. Dot and cross products are simple algebraic tools with direct geometric meaning. The dot product a · b equals |a||b|cos(theta), so it gives the cosine of the angle between two vectors when normalized; this is used to compute alignment or to project one vector onto another. The cross product a × b yields a vector perpendicular to both a and b with magnitude |a||b|sin(theta); in robotics it's used to compute normals, moments, and torques. A concrete example: if a sensor measures a surface normal and you need a tangent direction, cross products give you a perpendicular vector that lies in the tangent plane. A common misconception is confusing component-wise multiplication with dot product; remember dot is a scalar, cross is a vector. Takeaway: use dot to measure alignment and projection, use cross for perpendicular directions and torque computations. Beyond transforms, several matrix properties are important in robotics. The determinant of a rotation matrix should be 1; if it's not, the matrix encodes scaling or reflection and is not a valid pure rotation. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors satisfy Av = λv and are useful for analyzing system behavior, such as stability or principal directions. Singular value decomposition, A = U Σ V^T, decomposes a general matrix into orthogonal factors and singular values; SVD is commonly used in solving least-squares problems and in computer vision tasks like essential matrix decomposition. A concrete example: use SVD to compute a least-squares fit for a transform when you have noisy correspondences between frames. A common misconception is to assume eigenvectors always form a basis; this fails for defective matrices but is fine for symmetric and many practical matrices.
